subject: Tessier (1976)
object: Tessier (1976) proposed an anatomical classification of facial, craniofacial, and laterofacial clefts based on personal observations, using the orbit as the primary structure of reference. Fifteen cleft locations were distinguished, and the course of each through soft tissue and bone was described. Combinations of several cleft types and associated malformations were also discussed.

subject: Dasouki et al. (1988)
object: Dasouki et al. (1988) reported an 8-month-old girl born with symmetric bilateral oblique facial clefts and calcaneovarus foot deformity. Head CT showed severe bilateral ocular hypoplasia and normal brain parenchyma.

subject: Dasouki et al. (1988)
object: Dasouki et al. (1988) found a de novo balanced translocation between chromosome 1 and chromosome 22 in the peripheral blood karyotype of a girl with bilateral oblique facial clefts. They noted that a submicroscopic imbalance resulting from the translocation could not be ruled out, and they recommended chromosome studies in children with such rare malformations.

subject: Dasouki et al. (1988)
object: Dasouki et al. (1988) suggested that the pattern of anomalies seen in their patient would help distinguish oblique facial clefts from amniotic band disruption.

subject: Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994)
object: Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994) reported 4 Brazilian patients with oblique facial clefts and a strikingly similar facial appearance. Three of them had consanguineous parents. The authors suggested that the pattern of facial involvement and the overall clinical picture pointed to a unique dysmorphogenetic process. In some cases this could represent an oculomaxillofacial dysostosis.

subject: Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994)
object: Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994) noted that 3 of their 4 Brazilian patients with oblique facial clefts had consanguineous parents. The paper's title cites evidence for clinical variability and genetic heterogeneity.

subject: Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994)
object: Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994) stated that oblique facial clefts are rare and include types 2 to 6 of Tessier's classification.

subject: Saadi et al. (2011)
object: Saadi et al. (2011) showed that loss-of-function mutations in the SPECC1L gene are pathogenic for oblique facial clefts (ObFC), a unique class of facial malformations.

subject: Saadi et al. (2011)
object: Saadi et al. (2011) found that knockdown of a SPECC1L homolog in zebrafish produced a faceless phenotype with loss of jaw and facial structures. In Drosophila, knockdown phenocopied mutants in the integrin signaling pathway, which have cell-migration and cell-adhesion defects.

subject: Saadi et al. (2011)
object: Saadi et al. (2011) found that during mouse embryogenesis, Specc1l is expressed in the cells of the developing facial primordia, which proliferate and fuse to form the face. In mammalian cells, SPECC1L colocalized with both tubulin and actin. SPECC1L deficiency caused defective reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and abnormal cell adhesion and migration. The authors concluded that SPECC1L functions in actin-cytoskeleton reorganization and is required for proper facial morphogenesis.
